title: Why Some People Hear Music That Isn't Really Playing
summary:
Almost everyone has had a song stuck in their head. But some people hear music that sounds just as real as a song on the radio, even when no music is playing. Scientists call these musical hallucinations.

A hallucination is when the brain senses something that is not really there. Musical hallucinations are sometimes linked to hearing loss. One idea is that when the part of the brain that handles sound gets less information from the ears, it starts pulling music from a person's memory instead.

A new study in the Journal of Neurology looked more closely at this condition. Researchers from the Netherlands and the United Kingdom studied 80 people who hear music that is not there. Most were older adults, with an average age of 65. The participants answered questions about their experiences and took hearing tests and brain scans.

The scientists noticed some interesting patterns. People who had hearing loss that was worse in one ear usually heard the music as if it came from outside their heads. Most others heard it inside their minds.

Most of the songs were older music, not new hits. Religious songs were the most common type, reported 18 percent of the time. Earlier research also found that these songs were often holiday or children's songs. This suggests the brain may be reaching into long-term memory for tunes people learned when they were young.

For many participants, the music was hard to control and bothersome. Only about one in five could do anything to change it, such as playing real music to cover it up.

Treatment depends on the cause, and explaining the science to patients can help. The goal is to remove the shame some people feel about the condition, so they are more comfortable asking for help.
why_it_matters: Understanding why the brain creates music that is not there can reduce shame around the condition and help people get the right support.

background_read: The brain does not just receive sounds from the ears; it actively works to make sense of them and fill in gaps.
A part of the brain handles hearing, and when it gets less information from the ears, it may start producing sounds on its own.
An ordinary 'earworm' is a song stuck in your head that you know is not real, while a musical hallucination sounds like real music playing.
Scientists study people with this condition using questionnaires, hearing tests and brain scans to understand what causes it.
